scenes.narration: This diagram has four distinct health boundaries; each tells you something different about the workload. Begin on the left with the infrastructure and guest computers. EC2 system status checks evaluate the underlying host infrastructure, while instance status checks evaluate the guest's reachability and configuration at a different layer. A pass at one layer does not prove all the others are healthy. The next purple panel compares EBS and application status. Attached EBS status checks help detect volume reachability or IO issues, while application checks need an explicitly configured HTTP or similar readiness signal. Now inspect the orange Auto Scaling section. Choose the appropriate health-check sources, such as supported EC2 and load-balancer health checks, and use a grace period that reflects actual startup behavior. Do not call the service healthy merely because the instance boots. Finally, the recovery panel distinguishes supported EC2 recovery for certain infrastructure failures from fleet replacement. Preserve the appropriate instance identity where recovery supports it, and collect in-guest memory and filesystem signals through an agent or custom metrics. The takeaway is to monitor the failure domain that matters to users, not one generic green status.

scenes.narration: This slide shifts from adding instances to removing them without harming users. On the left, several client requests enter a load balancer and are distributed to targets. One orange target is being removed. Target-group deregistration delay helps existing supported requests and connections drain within configured limits, while new eligible requests go to other targets. This is not an unlimited wait and long-running connections require application-aware handling. Next inspect the top-right panel. Auto Scaling scale-in protection can shield selected instances from certain group scale-in decisions, but does not prevent every termination path or replacement action. Now follow the middle-right queue-worker sequence. Workers should stop taking new tasks, complete or checkpoint the current work, and return unfinished messages to a retry-safe queue. The bottom-right checklist covers termination policies and lifecycle hooks, which coordinate bounded cleanup. Test shutdown while long requests run, while instances fail, and while new application versions deploy. A successful scale-in is not defined by reducing the count; it is defined by preserving service, requests and durable work.

scenes.narration: The four numbered panels explain why mixing instance sizes improves capacity choice but requires precise measurement. First, a mixed-instances Auto Scaling policy can draw from several eligible instance types and combine On-Demand with Spot purchasing. This creates flexibility across capacity pools, but does not mean every instance is identical. The second panel shows instance requirements or overrides and a software image. Check CPU architecture, runtime dependencies, memory and networking compatibility before putting several families in one group. Now examine the balance scale in the third panel. One smaller instance may represent one weighted capacity unit while a larger supported instance represents four. If weighted capacity expresses processing ability, then desired capacity, utilization and scaling metrics must use compatible units; counting machines without regard to weight can produce misleading behavior. Finally, the last panel combines capacity policy, rebalance and recovery. Keep an appropriate On-Demand baseline for business-critical work and diversify interruptible Spot allocation where justified. Test what happens when one pool loses capacity. The exam lesson is that capacity weight is a workload-specific unit, not an arbitrary number.

scenes.narration: This final architecture case brings the EC2 module decisions together. Read the first numbered panel: begin by measuring which resource actually limits the workload. CPU, memory, storage IO and network capacity have different symptoms, so select compatible instance families and features using representative tests. In the second panel, a shared database sits above application instances spread across three Availability Zones. Durable state should live outside individually replaceable hosts, while the database and caches themselves need appropriate resilience and consistency. The third panel shows purchasing and a rising demand curve. Match On-Demand, discount commitments, Spot where interruption is tolerable, and scaling policies to the workload's steady baseline, expected peaks and startup times. The final checklist demands evidence. Test normal request volume, sudden bursts, controlled scale-in and failure events. Verify response latency, total cost, data safety and recovery objectives. A configuration that looks correct on paper is not enough if a single failed dependency blocks every AZ. The professional architect answer is a measurable design whose capacity choices and recovery behavior can be demonstrated.
